Supervisor's note, biology lab, Zurich exchange programme, week 2.
Noor arrived at Monday's group meeting at 9:32 for a 9:00 start, smiling, with coffee. The room had already moved on to the second item. Two of the local students exchanged a look, and afterwards one of them asked me, quietly, whether Noor could be trusted with the shared incubator schedule. I asked Noor to stay back. Noor looked genuinely puzzled: at home, Noor said, a nine o'clock meeting usually begins when the senior arrives. When I explained that here half an hour late reads as not caring, Noor went red and went very quiet.
Shankar, our technician, who came from Chennai years ago, offered a tip: set the watch ten minutes fast and message the group if the tram is late. On Thursday the tram was late. At 8:52 the group got Noor's message: "Tram stuck, arriving 9:07, sorry." Nobody minded at all.

qa.q: What time did Noor arrive at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Noor arrived at 9:32 for a 9:00 start.

qa.q: How did Noor feel on learning how the lateness was seen?
qa.a: Noor was puzzled at first and then embarrassed, going red and very quiet.

qa.q: Which two tips from Shankar helped, and why?
qa.a: Setting the watch ten minutes fast and messaging the group when late; together they respect the local clock and show care even when delays happen.

qa.q: How did the local students see Noor's late arrival?
qa.a: They took it as a sign Noor might be unreliable, even wondering whether Noor could be trusted with the incubator schedule.

grounding: It illustrates a student used to flexible timings who arrives half an hour late in a strict-time culture, is seen as unreliable, and learns to tell people ahead.

Tuesday, Berlin
I want to crawl under the duvet. Our project group met at the library at 4. I left the hostel at 4, because at home 4 means around 4:30 and everyone knows it. I walked in at 4:31 and they had already split the work. Jonas said, "We thought you weren't coming." Not angry, just flat. Somebody had taken my section. I spent the whole meeting feeling like the unreliable Indian girl, which is worse than being angry.
Afterwards Lakshmi di, who's in her second year here, walked me to the tram. She said she did the exact same thing in her first month and a professor stopped talking until she sat down. Her rule: in Germany, 4 means 3:55. And if you're even five minutes late, message.
So: new alarm, 3:40, labelled GERMAN FOUR. Tomorrow I'm going to ask for my section back. Nandini, the new punctual version.

qa.q: When did Nandini walk into the library meeting?
How did Nandini feel during the meeting, and why?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and small, like the unreliable girl, because the group had already split the work and someone had taken her section.

qa.q: What rule did Lakshmi di share, and why is it useful?
qa.a: In Germany 4 means 3:55, and message if even five minutes late; it helps Nandini match the local sense of time and avoid offence.

qa.q: How might Jonas have seen Nandini's late arrival?
qa.a: Jonas probably read it as not caring about the group, and felt unsure whether to count on her, which is why he said they thought she wasn't coming.

grounding: It illustrates a student used to flexible timings who arrives thirty minutes late in a strict-time setting, is seen as unreliable, and learns the local clock.

passage:
Mentor's note, product team, Bengaluru office, Thursday.
Jatin came to our fortnightly chat looking flat. On Tuesday, Zainab, our new manager from the Rotterdam office, reviewed his launch plan in the team call. She said, "The timeline is unrealistic and slide four is confusing. Please redo both." No softening, no "good effort". Jatin said he spent the evening thinking she regretted hiring him. His voice cracked when he repeated her words.
I asked what exactly she had criticised. He looked at his notes: the timeline and one slide. Nothing about him. I suggested he ask her directly what she meant and what she valued in the plan. He was nervous but did it on Wednesday. Zainab was surprised he had been upset. She said the market research was the best she'd seen in the team, and she just hadn't thought to say so. They agreed she would tell him what works too. Jatin left today smiling.

qa.q: What two parts of the plan did Zainab criticise?
qa.a: The timeline and slide four.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel after Tuesday's call, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt hurt and insecure, thinking she regretted hiring him, and his voice cracked when he repeated her words.

qa.q: How did the mentor help Jatin separate tone from content?
qa.a: By asking what exactly was criticised, which showed it was two parts of the plan and nothing about him, and by suggesting he ask Zainab about her intent.

qa.q: How did Zainab see her own feedback?
qa.a: She saw it as simple clarity about the plan and was surprised it had upset Jatin, since she valued his market research.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional hurt by a foreign manager's blunt feedback, who learns by asking about intent and separating tone from content.

passage:
Monday night
Klaus, my new manager, read my report today and said, in front of Ayesha, "This section is weak. The numbers do not support your conclusion." Then he went back to his coffee. I nodded like a doll and then cried in the office loo for ten minutes. At home, if a boss said that, it would mean you're about to be fired.
Ayesha found me there. She's worked with him a year. She said, "He said the same to me about my first three reports. It means he read it carefully." I didn't believe her.
So at five I did the terrifying thing and asked him: "When you said weak, did you mean the whole report or that section?" He looked puzzled. "That section only. The rest is good. Why?" Just like that.
I've written his exact words on a sticky note and underlined "that section". Tomorrow I fix the numbers. Aditi, still a bit bruised.

qa.q: What did Klaus say about the numbers?
qa.a: "The numbers do not support your conclusion."

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after Klaus's comment?
qa.a: Aditi felt hurt and frightened, crying in the office loo and fearing it meant being fired.

qa.q: Which step helped Aditi most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Klaus what he meant by weak, because it showed the criticism was only about one section and the rest was good.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Klaus's style after a year of working with him?
qa.a: Ayesha sees his bluntness as a sign he reads work carefully, not as an attack, so she tries to reassure Aditi.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional hurt by a foreign manager's blunt criticism who asks about intent and separates the tone from the content.

passage:
I'm Zubin, and I shared a desk with Ojas the month before our firm posted us both to Nairobi. What I saw was this: while I read travel blogs and assumed, Ojas asked. Every evening he messaged Wanjiru, a Kenyan colleague from the video calls, with small questions. How do people greet elders? Is it rude to refuse tea? Which hand do you use to give something? What should I bring when invited home? He wrote her answers in a little notebook. I teased him about it.
In Nairobi, at Wanjiru's family lunch, her grandmother held out her hand. Ojas took it in both of his, dipped his head, and gave the gift, a box of sweets, with his right hand. She said something in Kikuyu and everyone laughed warmly. I was standing there with my phone, not knowing what to do. I can't say what he felt. He looked calm.

qa.q: Where did Ojas write down Wanjiru's answers?
qa.a: In a little notebook.

qa.q: What might Ojas have been feeling at Wanjiru's family lunch, and what suggests it?
qa.a: He seemed calm and at ease; his steady greeting, taking the grandmother's hand in both of his, suggests his preparation made him feel confident.

qa.q: What did Ojas's approach get right that Zubin's did not?
qa.a: Ojas asked a local person about greetings, tea and gifts instead of assuming from blogs, so he knew how to show respect when it mattered.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru's grandmother have seen Ojas?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and warmed by a guest who greeted her properly, which is why the family laughed kindly.

grounding: It illustrates a worker who asks locals about greetings, gifts and customs before arriving, and how curiosity and humility win warmth.

"What should I know?" he asked. Budi explained: shoes off at the door, give and take with the right hand, don't touch anyone's head, and bring something small, like fruit. Lalit wrote it on his phone. His friend Madhav, on a call from Pune, laughed: "Just be yourself, yaar."

Week five: Budi's daughter got married, and Lalit was invited. Madhav, hearing this, said, "How are you already on wedding lists?"

The regional train from Munich to Nuremberg was already forty minutes late, and Zubin and his colleague Hrithik had squeezed into the only two free seats, in the quiet carriage. Hrithik's phone rang. It was his mother, and he answered on speaker, loudly: "Haan Mummy, haan, khaana kha liya!" Zubin saw a woman opposite lower her book and stare. A man across the aisle pointed at the little sign showing a crossed-out phone.
Zubin's cheeks went warm. He leaned over. "Hrithik, quiet coach. Take it in the corridor?" Hrithik looked startled, then grinned and went. Zubin turned to the woman. "Sorry, his mother calls every day. It's a kind of love, just loud." She smiled, and so did the man. When Hrithik came back, he whispered, "Why didn't anyone tell me?" The train crawled on. Zubin sent him a photo of the sign.

qa.q: What did the little sign across the aisle show?
qa.a: A crossed-out phone.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when the woman lowered her book and stared?
qa.a: Zubin felt embarrassed, his cheeks going warm, aware that Hrithik's loud call was bothering the passengers.

qa.q: Which of Zubin's two moves helped, and why?
qa.a: Quietly asking Hrithik to take the call to the corridor, and kindly explaining to the woman that it was a caring mother; this eased both sides without shaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have seen the moment?
qa.a: Hrithik seemed surprised and a little sheepish, not having known about the quiet coach, and grateful someone told him kindly.

Together they went to the coordinator. Usha said politely, "I'd like to try rebuttals. I'm not very loud." The coordinator paused, then nodded. "Fair. Rebuttals it is."

qa.a: Rebuttals.

qa.a: Finding Rekha, who had faced the same thing, gave her support, and together they gently corrected the coordinator by asking for the role that fitted her.

passage:
Dear Yamini didi,
Three weeks at the new school in Delhi. You asked how it is, so here's the truth. On day one, Rohan said, "You're Gujarati, so you'll be selling us something, right?" and everyone laughed. Since then, every time I bring thepla, it's "the Gujju tiffin". The teacher asked me to do the class accounts "because you people are good at business." I'm not. I'm good at drawing. I felt like nobody even knew my name, just my state.
Last Friday I tried something. When Rohan said it again, I said, "My dad's a teacher and I can't add. Try another joke." It came out calm, somehow. A few people laughed with me, not at me. And a boy called Imran said he's tired of "all Biharis are like this" jokes too. We sat together at lunch. He draws comics.
Write back soon.
Darshan

qa.q: What is Darshan actually good at?
qa.a: Darshan is good at drawing.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel in the first weeks, and why?
qa.a: Darshan felt unseen and frustrated, as if nobody knew Darshan's name, only Darshan's state, because of the jokes and assumptions.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that helped?
qa.a: Darshan corrected Rohan calmly with a light, true reply, and then found a supportive peer in Imran who faced similar jokes.

qa.q: How might Imran see the jokes in class?
qa.a: Imran is tired of being labelled too, and probably felt relief finding someone who understood.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager treated as a state stereotype who feels unseen, gently corrects it and finds a supportive peer.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Ira, thanks for having me on the school podcast. So, I'm Farhan, sixteen, and when we moved to Bengaluru from the old city in Hyderabad, the first thing a classmate said was, "People from your side of town are all hot-headed, na?" Like a joke. But then every time I spoke up in class, someone would say, "Here comes the temper." I stopped speaking up. I just wanted them to see me, not a map. What changed? Two things. First, I said once, quite calmly, "I'm actually the calmest one in my family. Ask my mum." People laughed, but it stuck. Second, I joined the robotics club, and there nobody cared where I came from, just whether my code worked. My friends there call me Farhan, not Hyderabad. That made the difference.

qa.q: What did the robotics club care about?
qa.a: Just whether Farhan's code worked.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when classmates said "Here comes the temper"?
qa.a: Farhan felt unseen and discouraged, so Farhan stopped speaking up in class.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's two steps would you advise another new student to try first?
qa.a: A calm, gentle correction like Farhan's, because it challenges the label without a fight, and then looking for a group like the robotics club where people judge you by what you do.

qa.q: How might Ira react to Farhan's story as the host?
qa.a: Ira might feel sympathetic and curious, perhaps recognising the same kinds of jokes from their own school.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reduced to a label about their area who feels unseen, gently corrects it and finds supportive peers.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
Saturday night
Watched three films this week for the holiday, and I've started seeing something. I can't unsee it. In all three, the maid was dark-skinned and from a village, and her job was to cry or be funny. The villain in two of them had a thick southern accent. The only guy in a skullcap was a gangster. Pooja said I'm overthinking it, it's just a film. Maybe. But then we played a game: who is missing? We looked at the hero's friends. No one in a wheelchair. No one from the northeast. No women engineers, even though Pooja's mum is one.
It's weird, I felt angry and also kind of relieved, like I'd found a hidden trick. Tomorrow's film is Pooja's pick. I'm going to count again. Kiran, film detective.

qa.q: What game did Kiran and Pooja play?
qa.a: "Who is missing?"

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after noticing the patterns?
qa.a: Kiran felt angry and also kind of relieved, like finding a hidden trick.

qa.q: Why is asking "who is missing?" a useful habit?
qa.a: It turns watching into noticing, helping Kiran spot which groups are left out or shown only as villains, maids or jokes.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Kiran's new habit?
qa.a: Pooja first thought Kiran was overthinking, but joining the game and noticing that engineers like Pooja's own mum were missing suggests Pooja is starting to see it too.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who notices films casting certain groups as villains, servants or comic relief and starts asking who is missing.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: On Sunday evenings the panchayat hall in Raipur Kalan showed an old film on a borrowed projector, and Divyansh, fourteen, never missed it. This week, halfway through, he nudged his cousin Deepika. "Why is the villain always the dark one with the moustache who talks like the people from our side?" Deepika, who was studying to be a teacher, raised her eyebrows at him. "Keep watching. Count." He counted: the servant spoke like his grandmother; the comedian was a fat man from a village; the smart people all spoke English. Walking home under the neem trees, he said, "There's nobody like us who is a doctor in it." Deepika nodded. "So who's missing from the story?" Divyansh thought about the kind district doctor who had stitched his arm. "Him," he said. He went quiet, a little angry, but thinking hard.

qa.q: Where were the films shown?
qa.a: In the panchayat hall in Raipur Kalan, on a borrowed projector.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: He was a little angry at what he noticed, but curious and thinking hard.

qa.q: How did Deepika help Divyansh think critically?
qa.a: She did not lecture; she asked him to count and then asked who was missing, so he found the pattern himself.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Divyansh's questions?
qa.a: Deepika probably felt pleased and proud that her cousin was starting to watch with open eyes.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who starts to spot patterns in how films show villains, servants and comics, and begins asking who is missing.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Uma, sit, your Uday Thatha will tell you something about himself that's not so nice. I was twenty, on the Madras bus to college. A man got on in a torn lungi, smelling of fish, and sat next to me. I pulled my bag closer to my chest. I was sure he'd try to steal it. My whole body went stiff. Then the conductor dropped a ticket book, and this man picked it up and read out the page numbers in perfect English to help. He was a teacher, going to the market for his mother. I felt hot in the face. I had judged him by his clothes in three seconds. I didn't punish myself for years, but I didn't forget either. After that, whenever I felt that stiffness, I asked myself: what do I actually know? Often, nothing.

qa.q: How did the man help the conductor?
qa.a: He picked up the dropped ticket book and read out the page numbers in perfect English.

qa.q: What was young Uday feeling when the man sat next to him?
qa.a: He felt suspicious and uneasy, his body stiffening and holding his bag close.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Thatha's story, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: Seeing the man help the conductor showed him he had judged by clothes; afterwards he asked himself what he actually knew whenever he felt that stiffness.

qa.q: How might the man in the lungi have felt if he noticed Uday clutching his bag?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt or tired of being treated as a thief because of his clothes.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who notices he assumed a stranger would behave a certain way because of dress, and names the bias honestly without self-punishment.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: The night bus from Manali broke down near a dhaba at 2 a.m., in pouring rain, and the driver said it would take an hour. Lokesh, twenty, got off and stood under the tin roof. A young woman with a shaved head, tattoos up both arms and a heavy leather jacket stood nearby. Lokesh moved a step away without thinking. He expected her to be rude or trouble. Then an old man slipped on the wet steps. She was there first, holding his elbow, then asked the dhaba owner for a dry chair. "I'm Pema," she said later, handing Lokesh a cup of tea. "Nurse in Delhi." Lokesh took the tea and felt uneasy about that step he'd taken. He didn't make a big speech to himself. He just noticed it: tattoos, rude. Where did that come from? The bus coughed back to life.

qa.q: What was Pema's job?
qa.a: A nurse in Delhi.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when Pema handed him tea?
qa.a: Lokesh felt uneasy and a little embarrassed about the step he had taken away from her.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do with his mistake that was healthy?
qa.a: He noticed the assumption honestly and asked where it came from, without punishing himself or making a big speech.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pema when strangers step away from her?
qa.a: It may feel tiring and a bit hurtful, being judged by her tattoos and jacket before she has said anything.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who notices he assumed a stranger would behave badly based on dress, and names the bias honestly without self-punishment.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: On her first week at the Chennai software office, Ganga was paired with Lakshmi, who wore a simple cotton sari, oiled plait and a small bindi, and spoke softly in Tamil to the security guard. Ganga, twenty-one, caught herself thinking: she won't know the new testing tool; I'll have to carry her. When the build broke on Thursday, Ganga panicked. Lakshmi read the log for thirty seconds, said, "Missing dependency, line forty," and fixed it. Ganga felt her face go warm. She hadn't said anything unkind, but she'd thought it. At lunch she admitted to herself, not with drama, that she'd judged Lakshmi by her clothes and her quietness. She didn't beat herself up. She just asked Lakshmi, "Can you show me how you read logs so fast?" Lakshmi smiled and pulled up a chair.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi say was wrong with the build?
qa.a: "Missing dependency, line forty."

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when Lakshmi fixed the build?
qa.a: Ganga felt embarrassed, her face going warm, because she had assumed Lakshmi would need carrying.

qa.q: What did Ganga do well after noticing her bias?
qa.a: She admitted it to herself honestly without beating herself up, and then asked Lakshmi to teach her, turning the moment into respect.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt when Ganga asked to learn from her?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt pleased and respected, and perhaps unaware she had ever been underestimated.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who notices she assumed a colleague's skill from dress and manner, and names the bias honestly without self-punishment.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Jyoti, you're scared of failing that exam because everyone expects you to top? Let me, your Uma masi, tell you about when I was nineteen, in engineering college. The professor would say in class, "Our Uma is from a family of mathematicians, she'll solve it," and the boys would say, "Your people are born with calculators." It felt like praise. But it was a cage. When I got my first C, I couldn't eat. I hid the paper in my mattress. I thought failing meant I wasn't myself anymore. One day I finally said to the professor, very politely, "Sir, I'm not born good at maths. I work hard at it, and sometimes I get it wrong." He looked surprised, then said, "That's fair." After that I could ask questions in class without feeling like a fraud. My marks actually improved.

qa.q: Where did young Uma hide the paper with the C?
qa.a: In her mattress.

qa.q: How did young Uma feel when she got her first C?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and trapped, unable to eat, as if failing meant she wasn't herself anymore.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Uma masi's story?
qa.a: Politely telling the professor she wasn't born good at maths but worked hard; it freed her to ask questions and her marks improved.

qa.q: How might the professor have seen his own praise?
qa.a: He probably thought he was being kind and encouraging, and was surprised to learn it had felt like pressure.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult praised as naturally good at maths because of family and community, who feels unable to fail and corrects it kindly.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
The mechanics exam was in two hours and the hostel's power had gone out. Aditi, nineteen, sat on the steps with a torch, trying to revise, her stomach tight. Last week Chinmay sir had handed back papers and said, "Aditi's people never fail. Hardworking community." Since then she hadn't slept properly. Her last test had been average, and she'd hidden it from everyone. What if she failed this one, in front of everyone who expected her not to?
When the power came back and she reached the exam hall, early, Chinmay sir was there. Her voice shook. "Sir, can I say something? I'm not hardworking because of where I'm from. I just work. And I can fail." He looked at her for a long moment. "You're right. That was careless of me. Do your best." She went in feeling lighter, though her hands still trembled.

qa.q: What did Chinmay sir say when handing back the papers?
qa.a: "Aditi's people never fail. Hardworking community."

qa.q: How had Aditi been feeling since Chinmay sir's comment?
qa.a: She felt pressured and anxious, unable to sleep properly, afraid to fail when everyone expected her not to.

qa.q: What did Aditi do, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: She kindly but clearly told Chinmay sir that she works hard as herself, not because of community, and that she can fail; it freed her from the box before the exam.

qa.q: How did Chinmay sir see his comment after Aditi spoke?
qa.a: He realised it was careless, admitting she was right, which suggests he had meant it as praise without seeing the pressure.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult praised as hardworking because of her community, who feels unable to fail and corrects it kindly.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: In the college canteen in Mumbai, Sarita's friends were planning a quiz team. "Sarita's from Kerala, she'll top the science round," said Neel. "You people are born toppers." They laughed, and Sarita laughed too, but her chest tightened. She had nearly failed chemistry last term and told no one. For weeks she'd been studying until two, terrified of being the Malayali who wasn't clever. Sabina, sitting beside her, noticed Sarita's smile didn't reach her eyes. Later, walking to the station, Sabina asked, "You okay with that 'born toppers' thing?" Sarita let out a long breath. "No. It's like I'm not allowed to be bad at anything." Sabina nodded. "Then say so." The next day, when Neel repeated it, Sarita said, lightly, "I'm from Kerala and I'm terrible at chemistry. Put me in the music round." Everyone laughed, and she meant it.

qa.q: Which round did Sarita ask to be put in?
qa.a: The music round.

qa.q: How had Sarita been feeling about the "born toppers" comments?
qa.a: She felt pressured and afraid, her chest tightening, as if she wasn't allowed to be bad at anything.

qa.q: How did Sabina support Sarita?
qa.a: Sabina noticed her forced smile, asked privately whether she was okay, and encouraged her to say so, which helped Sarita correct it kindly.

qa.q: How might Neel see his comment?
qa.a: Neel probably thought it was a compliment and a joke, without realising it put pressure on Sarita.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult praised as a natural topper because of her region, who feels unable to fail and corrects it kindly with a friend's support.
